task.title: Put a drawing in your document
task.shortdesc: You write a drawing in your XML, or you show a drawing from a file. Then you set its size and its scale, and you place it in the text.

step.cmd: Write the drawing in your XML

info.p: Add an svg element in the SVG namespace where the drawing must appear. CSSMedia draws it as a replaced element on the line of the text that surrounds it.

stepxmp.pre: <para>The mark <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="24" height="24"> <circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10" fill="#cfe3f5" stroke="#1d4f7a" stroke-width="2"/> </svg> stays on its line.</para>

info.p: You can declare the namespace with a prefix instead, as in <s:svg xmlns:s="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">. An svg element in another namespace is an ordinary element of your XML, and CSSMedia does not draw it.

The width and height attributes of the svg element give the size of the drawing. A number is a length in pixels, and you can use units, such as 5cm or 1in. A rule of your style sheet with width or height wins over the attributes:
A drawing without a size is 300 pixels wide and 150 pixels high. When it has a viewBox and you set only the width or only the height, CSSMedia takes the other size from the proportion of the viewBox.

step.cmd: Scale the drawing with a viewBox

info.p: The viewBox attribute holds four numbers: the x and y of the top left corner of the area you draw in, and its width and height. CSSMedia scales that area to fill the size of the drawing, so you can draw with the numbers that suit the picture, whatever size it has on the page.
When the area and the drawing have different proportions, preserveAspectRatio decides what happens. It has an alignment, from xMinYMin to xMaxYMax, and one of these words:

ul.li: meet is the default. The whole area is visible, and part of the drawing stays empty.
slice fills the drawing, and the parts of the area outside it are cut.

info.p: The value none stretches the area to the size of the drawing and ignores the proportions.

image.alt: Three boxes of the same size that show the same circle. With meet the whole circle is visible and the box has empty space at the sides. With slice the circle fills the box and its top and bottom are cut. With none the circle is stretched into an ellipse that fills the box.

stepxmp.pre: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="60" viewBox="0 0 50 50" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"> <circle cx="25" cy="25" r="25" fill="#cfe3f5" stroke="#1d4f7a"/> </svg>

info.p: An svg element is inline, like a word. Set display: block to put the drawing on a line of its own. A drawing has margins, padding and borders like any other box:

step.cmd: Show a drawing from a file

info.p: Give an element the file as its content, as Place an image explains for every image. The size of the file is the one in its svg element, and you can set another size with width and height:

A file is a document of its own. It has its own styles: style elements, style attributes and style sheets linked with an xml-stylesheet processing instruction. The style sheet of your document does not reach it.

If CSSMedia cannot read a file, or the file is not an SVG document, it does not draw it and names the file in the messages at the end of the run. An image that contains itself is reported in the same way.

Inside a drawing, the image element shows a file with the href attribute, and it can be a PNG, JPEG or WebP image, or another SVG file. Its x, y, width and height give the area it fills, and preserveAspectRatio fits the image in that area as it does for a viewBox.
